name: cislunar-dynamics
description: Restricted Earth-Moon mission model for Artemis II style cislunar flyby lessons. The domain reconstructs one nominal mission family from launch through high Earth orbit, translunar injection, lunar flyby, free-return coast, entry interface, and splashdown. Public trajectory functions come from one continuous launch-to-splashdown state integration and are cached by flyby-altitude family.

implementation.model: Single cached mission formulation. A continuous ODE integrates spacecraft position and velocity from launch through splashdown under Earth gravity, moving Moon gravity, and smooth tracking acceleration toward a NASA-timed nominal Artemis II reference family. The reference family preserves launch, Earth-orbit setup, translunar injection, lunar flyby, free return, entry interface, and splashdown timing anchors without switching the public trajectory between separate segment solvers.
implementation.integrator: Fourth-order Runge-Kutta (RK4) for the full launch-to-splashdown mission state.
implementation.stepSize: dt = 90 s for the cached mission solve. Public function lookup uses linear interpolation between cached samples.
implementation.storage: Per-flyby family trajectory arrays store day, position, and velocity samples for the full mission from day 0 through splashdown. Derived scalar functions reuse the same cached mission solve.
implementation.cache: Cache key is the rounded flyby-altitude family in statute miles, rounded to the nearest 50 mi. All public functions share the same cache for a given family.
implementation.coordinateSystem: Earth-centered 2D cislunar plane in kilometers. Public position functions return scene units where 1 unit = 10,000 km. Earth is centered at (0,0). The Moon position is time-dependent and uses a mean orbital period of 27.321661 days.

missionAnchors.launchToOrbit: Launch, initial insertion orbit, safe orbit, high Earth orbit, Orion separation, proximity ops, and departure setup are timed to the NASA Artemis II press kit.
missionAnchors.tli: Translunar injection occurs at mission day 1.067.
missionAnchors.flyby: Lunar SOI entry, closest approach, and SOI exit are aligned to the published Artemis II nominal timeline. Flyby altitude family is controlled by the flyAlt slider or explicit function argument.
missionAnchors.return: Return correction windows, service module separation, entry interface, and splashdown are modeled on the NASA nominal mission timeline.

note: This domain supports both explicit function arguments and slider injection. If flyAlt is omitted when calling a public function, the domain reads the current scene slider with id `flyAlt` via `_init({ getSlider })`.

flyAlt.description: Target lunar flyby altitude family in statute miles. Rounded to the nearest 50 mi for cache reuse and nominal family selection.

missionX.description: Orion x-coordinate in scene units at mission day `day`.
missionX.returns: number — x-position in scene units where 1 unit = 10,000 km.

params.name: day
params.description: Mission day from launch. Clamped to [0, 9.1].

params.name: flyAlt
params.description: Optional flyby altitude family in statute miles. Defaults to slider `flyAlt` if omitted.

missionY.description: Orion y-coordinate in scene units at mission day `day`.
missionY.returns: number — y-position in scene units where 1 unit = 10,000 km.

params.name: flyAlt
params.description: Optional flyby altitude family in statute miles.

missionVx.description: Approximate x-velocity in km/s from the mission solve.

missionVy.description: Approximate y-velocity in km/s from the mission solve.

moonX.description: Moon x-coordinate in scene units at mission day `day`.

moonY.description: Moon y-coordinate in scene units at mission day `day`.

moonTheta.description: Moon orbital phase angle in radians for the active mission family.

distEarthKm.description: Distance from Orion to Earth center.

distMoonKm.description: Distance from Orion to Moon center.

missionSpeedKmS.description: Magnitude of Orion velocity from the cached mission state.

missionBlackout.description: Line-of-sight blackout test between Orion and Earth with the Moon as occluder.
missionBlackout.returns: number — 1 if the Moon blocks line of sight to Earth, else 0.

missionPhase.description: Human-readable high-level mission phase for the given mission day.

missionMilestone.description: Human-readable mission milestone bucket aligned to the NASA Artemis II nominal sequence.

TLI.markdown: The burn that raises a parking orbit's apogee out to the Moon's distance. In Artemis II, Orion's service module performs it after the Earth-orbit setup.
TLI.prompt: Explain the translunar injection burn: what it changes about the orbit and roughly how much delta-v it takes.

free-return trajectory.markdown: A figure-eight path around the Moon whose lunar flyby bends the trajectory back toward Earth with no major burn — a built-in safe return if an engine fails.
free-return trajectory.prompt: Explain the free-return trajectory and why it is a safety choice for a crewed flyby.

gravity assist.markdown: A flyby that bends a spacecraft's path using a body's gravity. Relative to the Moon the speed in and out is the same; relative to Earth the direction — and the speed — change.
gravity assist.prompt: Explain how a gravity assist changes a trajectory without burning propellant, and whose frame the speed is conserved in.

lunar flyby.markdown: Passing close to the Moon without orbiting or landing. Artemis II swings around the far side at a few thousand miles altitude.
lunar flyby.prompt: Explain what happens during Artemis II's lunar flyby.

SOI.markdown: The region where the Moon's gravity dominates the motion, radius about $66{,}000$ km, found from $r \approx a\,(m/M)^{2/5}$. Patched-conic models switch from Earth-centred to Moon-centred there.
SOI.prompt: Explain the Moon's sphere of influence and how patched-conic trajectory models use it.

rocket equation.markdown: $\Delta v = v_e \ln\dfrac{m_0}{m_f}$ — the velocity change available from burning propellant down from initial mass $m_0$ to final mass $m_f$. The logarithm is why staging pays.
rocket equation.prompt: Explain the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation and why its logarithm makes staging necessary.

delta-v.markdown: $\Delta v$ — the total change in velocity a vehicle can make, or a manoeuvre needs. Mission planning is a $\Delta v$ budget: every burn spends from it.
delta-v.prompt: Explain delta-v as the currency of spaceflight.

specific impulse.markdown: $I_{sp}$ — thrust per unit weight of propellant burned per second, in seconds. $v_e = I_{sp}\,g_0$: higher $I_{sp}$ gives more $\Delta v$ from the same propellant.
specific impulse.prompt: Explain specific impulse and how it links to exhaust velocity and the rocket equation.

staging.markdown: Dropping empty tanks and engines once their propellant is spent, so later burns don't have to accelerate dead mass. Each stage restarts the rocket equation with a lighter vehicle.
staging.prompt: Explain why rockets use stages, using the rocket equation.

SLS.markdown: NASA's heavy-lift rocket for Artemis. Block 1 has a core stage with four RS-25 engines, two five-segment solid rocket boosters, and the ICPS upper stage.
SLS.prompt: Explain the Space Launch System's configuration and what each part does.

SRB.markdown: Strap-on boosters burning solid propellant. SLS's two five-segment SRBs provide most of the thrust at liftoff and separate about two minutes in.
SRB.prompt: Explain solid rocket boosters and why SLS relies on them at liftoff.

RS-25.markdown: The hydrogen–oxygen engine of the SLS core stage — the former Space Shuttle main engine. Four of them run for the whole core-stage burn.
RS-25.prompt: Explain the RS-25 engine and its role on SLS.

ICPS.markdown: SLS Block 1's upper stage, powered by one RL10 engine. On Artemis II it performs the Earth-orbit setup burns before separating from Orion.
ICPS.prompt: Explain the ICPS and what it does on Artemis II.

Orion.markdown: NASA's crew spacecraft: a crew module, the European Service Module, and a launch abort system. Only the crew module returns to Earth.
Orion.prompt: Explain Orion's parts and which of them come home.

ESM.markdown: Orion's service module, built for ESA. It supplies propulsion, power, water and air, and its main engine performs the translunar injection burn.
ESM.prompt: Explain the European Service Module and what it provides Orion.

LAS.markdown: The tower on top of Orion that can pull the crew module away from a failing rocket. It is jettisoned once the rocket has climbed past the need for it.
LAS.prompt: Explain Orion's launch abort system and when it is used.

apogee.markdown: The point of an Earth orbit farthest from Earth's centre, where the spacecraft moves slowest.
apogee.prompt: Explain apogee and why burns there raise the opposite side of the orbit.

perigee.markdown: The point of an Earth orbit closest to Earth's centre, where the spacecraft moves fastest.
perigee.prompt: Explain perigee and what a perigee-raise burn does.

periapsis.markdown: The closest point of an orbit to whatever body it is centred on — perigee for Earth, perilune for the Moon.
periapsis.prompt: Explain periapsis and how it is used in describing a lunar flyby.

cislunar.markdown: The region between Earth and the Moon's orbit, where both bodies' gravity matters.
cislunar.prompt: Explain cislunar space and why trajectories there are harder to model than simple orbits.

LOX.markdown: The oxidizer for SLS's hydrogen engines, stored at about $90$ K; paired with liquid hydrogen (LH2) at about $20$ K.
LOX.prompt: Explain why hydrogen and oxygen engines need cryogenic propellants.

entry interface.markdown: The conventional altitude where atmospheric entry begins, about $120$ km ($400{,}000$ ft).
entry interface.prompt: Explain entry interface and why lunar-return entry is faster than a return from orbit.

heat shield.markdown: Orion's ablative shield, about $5$ m across, protects the crew module during a lunar-return entry at about $11$ km/s.
heat shield.prompt: Explain how Orion's heat shield handles a lunar-return entry.
